issues.issue: The Preamble equates "Fund" with "Plan" as a single defined term, whereas Sections 1.20 and 1.22 define "Plan" as the rules of benefits and "Fund"/"Trust Fund" as the pool of assets. A court asked which meaning governs a reference to the "Fund" would have to reconcile the Preamble with those definitions.

The recital says the Collective Bargaining Agreements "establish the Plan," but Section 1.20 and Section 7.2(2) give the Board alone the design and adoption of the Plan. A party could argue the recital controls and makes the bargained agreements the source of Plan terms.

The recital contemplates that "the Union and the Association will execute a Trust Agreement and appoint Trustees," while Section 3.3 and the Preamble treat the named individuals as parties and Section 3.1 splits selection between Association and Union. A court could be asked whether the Association's and Union's appointment power derives from the recital or the operative sections.

The recital limits the Trust to the "exclusive purpose of providing pension and retirement benefits," while Section 4.1(a) and Section 2.2 permit "such other related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine." A party could argue the recital's narrower statement of purpose controls the operative benefit power.

The recital rests the amendment power on "Paragraph 18 of the Trust Agreement," a provision that has no counterpart in the restated instrument, whose amendment power is Section 10.1 and requires a unanimous Board vote plus three provisos. A court would have to decide whether the recited authority or Section 10.1 governs the validity of this restatement and later amendments.

Defining "Administrator" to include the Board itself cannot be squared with Article 7, which allocates distinct responsibilities to "The Administrator" (7.1) and "The Board" (7.2), or with Section 5.3(c), which has the Board engage a person as Administrator. Whether a duty assigned to the Administrator is a duty of the Board turns on which reading prevails.

The definition names the "Publishers' Association of New York," omitting "City," while the Preamble and Section 12.8(d) name the "Publishers' Association of New York City." The mismatch leaves the identity of the defined "Association" open on the face of the instrument.

"Both the Chairman and Secretary of the Board" is ambiguous as to whether the two officers constitute a single Authorized Person who must act jointly or are each separately authorized. The same sentence then adds "any individual Trustee ... duly authorized by the Board," which points the other way.

"Such other person or entity who, as a result of his relationship to the Covered Employee, is entitled under the terms of the Plan" states no boundary on what relationship qualifies and is circular, deferring entirely to the unstated Plan. The word "entity" also sits oddly against a definition keyed to a personal relationship.

The definition refers to the "Internal Revenue Code of 1936," a statute that does not exist; the sections cited throughout (401(a), 501(a), 404, 4975, 407) are provisions of the 1986 Code. The mechanical error leaves the governing statute unidentified on the face of the definition.

The definition counts an agreement as a "Collective Bargaining Agreement" only if it "is acceptable to the Board," which cannot be squared with Section 9.1, under which the contribution rate is "at all times" governed by the Collective Bargaining Agreements and their amendments and modifications regardless of Board approval. Whether a side memorandum modifying contribution rates binds the Fund depends on which provision controls.

The definition incorporates the Collective Trust's own agreement by reference "to the extent that the provisions thereof are not inconsistent with the terms of this Agreement," without saying who decides inconsistency or which term yields. A court would have to construe that proviso against the Collective Trust trustees' "sole and exclusive authority" granted in the same definition.

This definition requires a Committee to contain only "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee," while Section 5.6(b) requires "an equal number" of each. A Committee of one Employer and two Union Trustees satisfies Article 1 but violates Section 5.6(b).

"Covered under the terms of a Collective Bargaining Agreement ... requiring contributions on behalf of said individual" is circular and does not say whether coverage turns on the employee's job category designated under Section 2.4(c) or on contributions actually being owed. Employees in a unit for whom no contribution is in fact made fall in an undefined space.

The definition allows a broker-dealer to be selected as a "Corporate Trustee (as that term is defined in Section 3.12)," but Section 3.12(a) permits only "a bank or trust company located within the United States" to be appointed Corporate Trustee. The two provisions cannot both be given effect as to broker-dealers.

"Employer" is defined to mean any employer required to contribute under a Collective Bargaining Agreement, while Section 2.4 makes participation depend on the employer being "acceptable to the Trustees" and executing a Board-approved agreement. Whether an employer obligated by a bargaining agreement the Board never approved is an "Employer" cannot be answered from one provision alone.

The definition ties Employer Trustees to designation "pursuant to Section 3.3(a)," which names only two individuals, whereas successors are designated under Section 3.9 by certificate filed with the Board. The cross-reference leaves later Employer Trustees outside the literal definition.

"Foreign Securities" is defined by reference to ERISA Section 404(b) and 29 C.F.R. 2550.404b-1, which regulate where indicia of ownership of plan assets may be maintained rather than defining any category of security. The definition therefore supplies no usable boundary for the term used in Sections 1.21(h) and 5.5(p).

"Instructions" are defined as "written communications signed by an Authorized Person" yet expressly include telex and like transmissions that bear no signature, requiring only that the receiver can verify the sender "with a reasonable degree of certainty." Whether an unsigned electronic message is a valid Instruction is left ambiguous.

The definition makes a written acknowledgment of fiduciary status a condition of being an "Investment Manager," while Section 8.3 says only that the Board "may require" such a certificate. Whether a manager who never delivered the acknowledgment is an Investment Manager (and whether the Board's liability disclaimers in Sections 8.5 and 8.8 then apply) turns on that conflict.

The account is described as segregated "by the Trustees," while Section 8.1(b) directs the Board to segregate or to request the Custodian to segregate the assets. Whether assets a Custodian has segregated constitute an Investment Manager Account is left open.

"Plan" is defined as rules "from time to time adopted by the Board," which cannot be squared with the second recital's statement that the Collective Bargaining Agreements "establish the Plan." A dispute over whether bargained terms are Plan terms would require reconciling the two.

The eleven enumerated categories are prefaced by "including, but not limited to" and closed by catch-all subsection (k), so it is unclear whether an instrument unlike any listed item is a "Security." The ejusdem generis tension is sharpened by the express ERISA limits attached only to employer stock and employer obligations.

"Trust Fund" is limited to cash and property that "shall have been deposited" or is held by a Custodian, which says nothing about contributions due but unpaid that Article 9 elsewhere treats as owing "to the Trust Fund." Whether delinquent contributions are Fund assets cannot be answered from this definition.

The definition covers successors "and assigns" of a personal fiduciary office and conditions their status on appointment "as provided in Section 3.9 or Section 3.10," leaving unclear whether an individual can assign a trusteeship at all. The parenthetical condition also makes the definition read as though there are no Trustees until successors are appointed.

"Union" is defined to include "any affiliates thereof" without any test of affiliation, so which labor organizations can select Union Trustees or execute a Collective Bargaining Agreement under Section 1.8 is left open. The term matters wherever the Agreement gives the Union rights, as in Section 9.8 and Section 10.3(a)(2).

The definition ties Union Trustees to designation "pursuant to Section 3.3(b)," yet Section 3.8 provides that the Union Trustees "shall be" the incumbent officers of the Union and Section 3.10 governs successors. The three provisions give three different sources of Union Trustee status.

"Certain pension and related benefits" leaves "related benefits" undefined and unbounded, and "certain" gives no criterion for which pension benefits the exclusive purpose covers. Section 4.1(a) compounds the problem by leaving "related benefits" to the Board's determination.

The clause provides that anything inconsistent with Code Sections 401(a) and 501(a) means "this Agreement shall be deemed amended," which cannot be squared with Section 10.1, under which amendment requires a unanimous vote of the Board subject to three provisos. A court would have to decide whether an automatic deemed amendment can occur without the Section 10.1 process.

The ERISA "deemed amended" sentence conflicts with Section 10.1, which makes amendment of this Agreement depend on a unanimous vote of the Board, and it supplies no mechanism for determining what the deemed amendment says. Whether such a self-executing amendment is effective would have to be construed against Section 10.1.

Operating as a "jointly-administered" fund within Section 302(c) of the LMRA presupposes equal representation, but Section 3.1 composes the Board of two Employer Trustees and three Union Trustees. The two provisions cannot both be given literal effect.

Participation is conditioned on the Employer being "acceptable to the Trustees" and executing a Board-approved agreement, while Section 1.13 makes any employer required to contribute under a bargaining agreement an "Employer" without Board acceptance. Whether an unapproved employer participates in the Trust turns on which provision governs.

"An Employer shall be deemed to have" reviewed, adopted and agreed states no triggering act — no signature, contribution or other event is identified as producing the deemed agreement. Whether the deeming follows from Section 2.4 participation, from making a contribution, or from something else is unstated.

A Board of two Employer Trustees and three Union Trustees cannot be squared with Section 2.3's undertaking that the Trust be operated as a "jointly-administered" fund under LMRA Section 302(c), nor with Section 10.1(c)'s bar on amendments producing "unequal voting power" between the two groups. Amendment No. 4 later recomposed the Board as two and two, confirming the tension.

The named Association designees are superseded by Amendment No. 4's replacement of Section 3.3, which designates different individuals, so the section as printed no longer describes the Board. Which text governs at a given date must be worked out across the two instruments.

This subsection names three Union Trustees, while Amendment No. 4 replaces Section 3.3 with two Union designees and Amendment No. 4's Section 3.1 caps Union Trustees at two. The provisions cannot both be given effect.

Written appointments need only be provided to the Board "as soon as practicable after the appointments," a standard with no measurable boundary, while Section 3.11 vests a successor with full powers only upon designation and written acceptance filed with the Board. When a successor's authority begins is left uncertain.

Service continues until "death, incapacity, resignation or removal," but "incapacity" is undefined and no person or procedure is identified to determine it. Section 3.9 and 3.10 likewise speak of a Trustee who has "become incapable of acting" without a mechanism.

The final sentence deems a Trustee to have resigned when "the Contributing Employer which designated him" ceases to contribute, but under Sections 3.1 and 3.3(a) Employer Trustees are designated by the Association, not by any individual Contributing Employer. The deemed-resignation trigger cannot be applied to the Trustees this Agreement actually creates.

Although captioned "Removal," this section dictates that the Union Trustees "shall be" the incumbent president, vice president and secretary-treasurer, which cannot be squared with Section 3.1's grant of free selection to the Union or with Section 3.3(b)'s designation of named individuals. Section 3.10's successor mechanism, in which the principal officer designates, conflicts further.

The section says the principal officer "shall designate a successor Union Trustee" and in the same sentence that "a Successor Union Trustee shall be elected from the full-time officers of the Union." Designation and election are inconsistent methods, and the provision does not say which prevails.

Only "a bank or trust company located within the United States" may be appointed Corporate Trustee, while Section 1.12 defines "Custodian" to include broker-dealers "selected by the Board as a Corporate Trustee." The eligibility of a broker-dealer to serve in that role cannot be settled from either provision alone.

The power to let a Corporate Trustee hold the Fund "as sole trustee of a trust separate from the Fund created by this Trust Agreement" cannot be squared with Section 5.1, which vests the Board with all right, title and interest in the contributions and requires it to hold them in trust hereunder, or with Section 1.22's definition of the Trust Fund. Whether assets so transferred remain subject to this Agreement is left in doubt.

The declaration that the Trustees are "forever released and discharged from any responsibility or liability" for transferred assets cannot be squared with Section 5.7's prudent-person standard of care or with Section 7.2(4) and (13), which make the Board responsible for designating and monitoring fiduciaries. A court would have to decide whether the release survives those duties.

The prohibition on benefits "other than pension, retirement, and such other related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine" pairs enumerated specifics with an open catch-all the Board defines for itself, leaving the limitation without content. What counts as a "related" benefit is measured by nothing but the Board's own determination.

The Board is "fully protected" in acting "in reliance upon information received from the Contributing Employer" without any duty to verify, which sits against Section 9.9's audit machinery and Section 5.7's prudent-person standard. Whether reliance on an employer's erroneous status report is protected would require reading those provisions together.

The employer indemnity runs to "the consequences of relying on any information or directions furnished" with no limit of time, amount, causation or notice, and no requirement that the reliance have been reasonable. Its outer boundary is undefined on the face of the clause.

This section lets the Board "terminate the Plan (at any time)" acting alone, while Section 10.3(a) permits termination only by unanimous vote and written instrument, by joint resolution of the Union and the Association, or automatically. The two termination mechanisms cannot both be given effect.

Section 4.4 permits the Board to return contributions to an Employer, but Section 10.2 forbids any "return or diversion of any part of the Fund to any of the Contributing Employers" "except as otherwise provided in Section 10.3," and Section 10.3(b) forbids reversion "under no circumstances." Section 4.4 is nowhere excepted, so the two cannot be squared.

The closing sentence lets the Board "terminate or postpone any such benefit payments ... to the spouse, children and relatives of the person to whom any such benefits are payable," which cannot be squared with Section 5.2's command that the Board pay the benefits provided in the Plan or with Section 4.4's exclusive-benefit limitation. Whether an anti-alienation clause can authorize forfeiture of vested benefits is left open.

The Board is vested with all right, title and interest in "the Employer contributions made to the Trust," saying nothing about contributions due but unpaid that Article 9 authorizes it to sue for. Whether the Board holds title to unpaid contributions is not answerable from these words.

"All reasonable and necessary expenses" is followed by seven enumerated categories introduced by "including, but not limited to," leaving unclear whether an expense unlike any listed item is payable from the Fund. The enumeration's specificity invites an ejusdem generis reading against the general words.

This subsection allows the Board to "delegate such of its administrative duties" to persons, agents or organizations, while Section 5.13 permits delegation only of "ministerial powers or duties." Which delegations are authorized cannot be determined from either provision alone.

The powers are conferred "in its sole and absolute discretion" and expressly "free from any limitations imposed by state law on investments of trust funds," which cannot be squared with Section 5.7's requirement that the Board act with prudence and "diversify all Trust Fund Securities and other property to avoid the risks of large losses." Which standard measures an investment decision is left in doubt.

Subsection (y) authorizes "all acts (whether or not expressly authorized herein) which the Trustees may deem necessary and prudent," a catch-all standing against twenty-four minutely enumerated powers. Whether the specifics limit the general grant, or the general grant swallows them, is a classic ejusdem generis question.

The Board may delegate "one or more of its fiduciary responsibilities" to Committees, while Section 5.13 confines delegation to "ministerial powers or duties" and Section 7.2(5) reserves fiduciary functions to the Board except as delegated. The scope of permissible committee delegation turns on reconciling these.

A Committee must have "an equal number of Employer Trustees and Union Trustees" here, but Section 1.10 requires only "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee." A one-to-two committee satisfies the definition and violates this subsection.

The liability shield opens with "Except as otherwise provided by ERISA," which leaves the scope of the exoneration undetermined on the face of the provision, and it does not address the co-fiduciary duties the Board retains under Section 7.2(5). What loss the remaining Trustees actually escape cannot be read off the clause.

The prudent-person and diversification duties imposed here cannot be squared with Section 5.5, which empowers the Board "in its sole and absolute discretion" and free of state-law investment limits, or with Sections 5.8, 5.9(b), 8.5 and 8.8, which disclaim responsibility for investment outcomes. Which provision measures the Board's conduct is a live question.

Treating an employer's writing as "conclusive evidence of the truth and accuracy of the statements therein contained," with "no duty to make any investigation or inquiry," cannot be squared with Section 5.7's prudence standard or with Section 9.9's audit obligation to determine "the accuracy and completeness of such contributions and reports." A dispute over an under-reported remittance would put the two against each other.

Entitlement to "rely conclusively" on professional opinions sits against Section 5.7's requirement of care, skill, prudence and diligence in exercising "any and all powers under this Agreement." Whether reliance displaces the standard of care is not resolved by either provision.

Charging the Trust Fund with "first liens as security and indemnification against any liabilities of any kind which the Trustees ... may incur" cannot be squared with Section 10.2 and Section 10.3(b), which bar diverting the corpus to any purpose other than the exclusive benefit of Covered Employees and proper administrative expenses. The breadth of "any liabilities of any kind" is what makes the two collide.

Exonerating Trustees from "any error of judgment or ... any loss arising out of any act or omission" cannot be squared with Section 5.7's affirmative standard of care or with Section 5.9(d)'s carve-out for fraud, willful misconduct and gross negligence. A court would have to decide whether the blanket exoneration or the standard of care governs a claimed breach.

The final exception reads "or except as may otherwise reimbursed by insurance," a sentence with the verb omitted, so it is unclear whether insurance recovery merely reduces the indemnity or defeats it altogether. Section 5.11's direction that insurance proceeds "may be used to satisfy the obligations set forth in Section 5.9" points the opposite way.

The mandatory "shall purchase and maintain" fiduciary insurance is qualified by "To the extent not precluded by ERISA," leaving the existence and scope of the duty undetermined by the clause itself. Nothing states the amount, coverage or duration required.

"All monies received by the Trustees hereunder shall be deposited" with FDIC- or SIPC-insured institutions cannot be squared with Section 5.1, which says the Board "may deposit all or a portion of such monies" with Custodians, or with Section 5.5(i) and (h), which permit other investments and pooling. Whether deposit with an insured institution is mandatory for all receipts is left in doubt.

Delegation is confined to "ministerial powers or duties," which cannot be squared with Section 5.6(a) (delegation of "fiduciary responsibilities" to Committees), Section 5.3(c) (delegation of administrative duties) or Section 5.5(r). The permissible scope of delegation depends on which of these controls.

The Board's construction of the Plan and this Agreement is declared "final and binding upon all parties affected thereby," which cannot be squared with Section 6.6's arbitration of questions the Board cannot decide or with Section 9.10's requirement that withdrawal-liability claims be resolved only by arbitration. Which forum has the last word is precisely what a party would litigate.

This section authorizes execution of documents by "The Chairman and Secretary" together, while Section 12.6 makes "[e]very certificate or other instrument executed by the Chairman of the Trustees" conclusive in favor of a person relying on it. Whether the Chairman alone can bind the Board turns on reconciling the two.

Officer terms "commence on the date of their election and continue[] until their successors are elected," yet nothing in Article 6 provides for how or when officers are elected. The provision therefore fixes a term measured by an event the instrument never regulates.

Special meetings may be called "by any four Trustees," but Section 3.1 creates a Board of only five Trustees and Amendment No. 4 reduces it to four, so the calling right is nearly or entirely illusory. The threshold cannot sensibly be applied to the Board the Agreement actually constitutes.

Telephone meetings require "proper advance notice (as prescribed by either paragraph (a) or (b) above)," but paragraph (a) prescribes no notice at all, only that the Trustees fix the time of quarterly meetings. The cross-reference gives no rule for regular meetings held by telephone.

A quorum of "two Union Trustees and two Employer Trustees" cannot be satisfied without the attendance of every Employer Trustee under Section 3.1 (which provides only two), and requires the entire Board under Amendment No. 4's two-and-two composition. That makes the quorum rule collide with Section 6.2's meeting machinery and with the deadlock provisions of Sections 6.4(d) and 6.6.

The subsection says in one sentence that all action is "by unanimous vote of the Trustees" and in the next that it is "by unanimous vote of the two units," which are different requirements where a Trustee dissents within his unit. Whether an individual Trustee can block Board action is left unresolved by the provision's own words.

Casting a unit's vote on "the concurring vote of a majority" of that unit cannot be squared with Section 6.4(a)'s statement that all action is taken "by unanimous vote of the Trustees," since a dissenting Trustee is bound by his unit's majority. Which sentence governs decides whether unanimity means unanimity of persons or of units.

Proxies are "valid only at the meeting immediately succeeding its execution," which does not say whether a proxy survives an adjournment or a meeting that fails for want of a quorum. "The meeting immediately succeeding" is ambiguous as between the next scheduled meeting and the next meeting actually held.

This subsection sends "any matter presented for decision by the Board" that deadlocks to arbitration, while Section 5.14 gives the Board "complete authority, in its sole and absolute discretion, to construe the terms of the Plan or this Agreement" with decisions "final and binding." Whether a deadlocked benefit or interpretation question goes to an arbitrator turns on reconciling the two.

The duty to submit a deadlocked question is placed on "the Chairman," who under Section 6.1(a) must "at all times" be a Union Trustee, so one side controls the trigger subject only to a Trustee's petition to the district court. Section 6.4(d), by contrast, says the deadlocked matter "shall then be resolved by arbitration" without any such gatekeeper.

Hearings are held in New York City "unless otherwise specifically agreed to by both parties," but the arbitration under Section 6.6 is between two units of a single Board, and the Agreement nowhere identifies who the "parties" to such an arbitration are. The term is left without a referent.

The opening sentence — "Where the Administrator is a Trust Fund, subject to the terms of this Agreement ..." — has no predicate and never states what the Administrator is responsible for, yet the enumerated duties depend on "[s]uch responsibilities." As written the source and extent of the Administrator's authority cannot be determined from the section.

Item (1) gives the Board "the right to amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time," which cannot be squared with Section 10.1's requirement of a unanimous vote subject to three provisos or with Section 10.3(a)'s termination mechanisms, including joint resolution of the Union and the Association. Whether the Board may terminate unilaterally depends on which provision controls.

The Board is given "exclusive power and authority to exercise the powers set forth in Section 5.5" over self-directed assets, duplicating Section 8.4(b), which states the same rule for assets as to which no Investment Manager has been appointed. The two overlapping grants leave unclear which governs assets an Investment Manager was appointed for but does not in fact manage.

The Board must "meet periodically" with each Investment Manager, a term with no stated interval or benchmark against which compliance could be measured. Section 7.2(13)'s monitoring duty likewise supplies no frequency.

This section makes the fiduciary acknowledgment optional ("may require"), while Section 1.18 makes a written acknowledgment to the Board a defining condition of being an "Investment Manager." Whether a manager without an acknowledgment is an Investment Manager, and thus whether the Board's disclaimers in Sections 8.5 and 8.8 apply to it, cannot be answered from either alone.

The Investment Manager receives the Section 5.5 powers "except subsections (3) through (y)," but Section 5.5 has no subsection numbered (3); its subsections run (a) through (y). The excepted range therefore cannot be identified, leaving the manager's powers indeterminate.

The disclaimer that neither the Board nor the Administrator is "responsible or liable for any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager" cannot be squared with Section 7.2(13)'s duty to "[m]onitor and evaluate" investment managers' performance or Section 7.2(15)'s duty to terminate them where necessary. Whether the Board can be held to those duties despite the disclaimer is a genuine question.

Making the Investment Manager's authority and terms of retention "the sole responsibility of the Board" cannot be squared with Section 8.5, which declares the Board not responsible or liable for any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager, or with Section 8.8's disclaimer. What responsibility the Board retains depends on which provision prevails.

The disclaimer that issuing guidelines is not "an acceptance by the Board of any investment management or supervisory powers" cannot be squared with Section 7.2(10), which requires the Board to formulate and implement general investment policies and to promulgate directions and guidelines. The provision denies the supervisory role another provision imposes.

This section makes the contribution rate governed "at all times" by the Collective Bargaining Agreements and their "amendments, supplements, and modifications," while Section 1.8 recognizes as a Collective Bargaining Agreement only one that "is acceptable to the Board." Whether a side memorandum reapportioning or altering the rate binds the Fund without Board acceptance cannot be answered from either provision alone.

"Amendments, supplements, and modifications" is left undefined, so it is unclear whether letter agreements, memoranda of agreement and reapportionment understandings between an Employer and the Union count as such. The final sentence's promise that nothing here changes "any of the terms or provisions of any such agreement" sharpens the question of what documents are in the set.

Contributions are effective "as of the date specified in the Collective Bargaining Agreement," while Section 2.4(b) makes participation effective on a date the Employer designates. Where the two dates differ, nothing says which governs the obligation to contribute.

The sentence that "[t]he costs and expenses incurred in the collection of Employer contributions shall be paid from the Fund" cannot be squared with Section 9.4(b), Section 9.5(b) and Section 9.7(d), which place those same collection costs, counsel fees and court costs on the delinquent Employer. Who ultimately bears collection costs turns on reconciling them.

The liquidated damage is "the greater of interest on, or twenty percent of, the unpaid contributions," but this subsection states no rate or period for the interest leg of the comparison. Section 9.5(b)'s 18 percent is a rate on "expenses incurred in effectuating such payment," not plainly the measure meant here.

The fixed 18 percent rate is replaced by Amendment No. 2, which adds "or such other interest rate that the Trustees deem appropriate," so the rate referred to by Sections 9.4(a) and 9.7(b) as "the method set forth in Section 9.5" is no longer fixed. Which text applies to a given delinquency period would have to be worked out across the two instruments.

"Several and not joint" is stated without qualification, leaving unclear whether it also disclaims the joint liability of trades or businesses under common control for the contributions and withdrawal liability that Sections 9.6 and 9.10 contemplate under ERISA. The reach of the disclaimer is not fixed by its own words.

The parenthetical "(hereinafter collectively referred to as 'unpaid contributions')" is attached to a list of agreements, rules and guidelines rather than to any sum of money, so the defined term has no coherent antecedent. Section 9.7 then awards "[a]ll unpaid contributions due and payable" in reliance on that defined term.

Interest is to be "computed in accordance with the method set forth in Section 9.5," but Section 9.5(b) states only a flat rate on collection expenses, and as amended leaves the rate to the Trustees' discretion. There is no "method" in Section 9.5 to which this computation can be referred.

This section preserves the right of "the Union, the Plan, the Trust Fund, the Board, or any Committee" to enforce contribution obligations "in any other type of proceeding," while Section 9.10 forbids withdrawal-liability claims from becoming "the subject of litigation in the courts." Which controls a dispute that is both a contribution claim and a withdrawal-liability claim is unresolved.

The Employer must produce "all records deemed necessary by such persons," a scope fixed by the auditor's own judgment with no objective limit, and the Board "may charge an Employer for the cost" without stating any condition such as a finding of underpayment. Both the reach of the audit and the cost-shifting trigger are left undefined.

The mandatory arbitration reaches only "claims by third parties (including Employers) against the Trust Fund concerning the assessment ... of withdrawal liability," leaving open whether an employer's declaratory or contract action about the contribution base, or a claim brought by the Fund, falls within it. The final sentence, preserving the Fund's right to sue in court, deepens the asymmetry.

The proviso that an amendment must not be "inconsistent with the purposes for which the Fund was established" supplies no benchmark, and the purposes are stated differently in the third recital (pension and retirement benefits) and in Section 2.2 (pension and "related" benefits). Whether a given amendment satisfies the proviso cannot be measured from this clause.

The ban on any amendment producing a "return or diversion of any part of the Fund to any of the Contributing Employers" is excepted only "as otherwise provided in Section 10.3," but Section 10.3(b) forbids reversion outright and it is Section 4.4 that authorizes the return of mistaken or nondeductible contributions. The cross-reference points to a provision that grants no exception.

Termination is committed to unanimous Board vote, joint resolution of the Union and the Association, or automatic operation, which cannot be squared with Section 7.2(1)'s statement that the Board has "the right to amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time" or Section 4.2's power to terminate the Plan at any time. Who may end the Trust depends on which provision governs.

"Under no circumstances shall any portion of the corpus or income of the Trust Fund ... revert or accrue to the benefit of any Employer" cannot be squared with Section 4.4, which permits the Board to return mistaken, disqualified or nondeductible contributions to the Employer. A refund demand would put the two provisions directly against each other.

The Board's records are made "the official records of the Plan and Trust Fund for all purposes," which sits against Section 9.9, under which an Employer's payroll and wage records are audited to determine the accuracy of contributions. In a contribution dispute the two provisions point to different controlling records.

Valuation is to be at fair market value "computed in accordance with such commercially acceptable valuation method or methods determined by the Board," so the standard is set by the very party whose valuations are at issue and "commercially acceptable" is undefined. Because Section 11.2 governs valuation "[f]or all purposes of this Agreement," the vagueness carries into asset and liability computations.

"The New York City metropolitan area" has no fixed boundary — it is commonly read to include parts of New Jersey and Connecticut — yet the Board "shall be deemed to be located at that address" though no address is given. Situs matters for Section 12.2's choice of law and for venue under Sections 6.6 and 9.10.

The direction that the Agreement "shall not be construed by reference" to titles and headings cannot be squared with Section 1.12, which defines "Corporate Trustee" "as that term is defined in Section 3.12" — a term appearing only in that section's heading, "Use of Corporate Trustee." Giving effect to this section would strip meaning from that definition.

Making "[e]very certificate or other instrument executed by the Chairman of the Trustees" conclusive cannot be squared with Section 5.15, which authorizes execution by "[t]he Chairman and Secretary" or by a resolution-designated pair of Union and Employer Trustees. Whether a third party may rely on the Chairman's signature alone turns on reconciling them.

Importing every word defined in the Plan into this Agreement cannot be squared with Article 1, which independently defines the same key terms ("Plan," "Covered Employee," "Beneficiary," "Employer"), since the Plan is a document the Board may amend unilaterally under Section 4.2. Whether a Plan definition can override an Article 1 definition is left to the words "except as otherwise expressly provided herein."

The addresses and the designation of a "Fund Administrator" here are superseded by Amendment No. 1 and Amendment No. 3, which substitute a "Fund Director" and new addresses. Which notice text is operative for a given communication must be determined across the three instruments.

The provision as printed begins in the middle of a sentence — "the Board) or any person claiming by or through them" — with no subject identifying whose rights are being denied. As written, the class of persons who "shall [not] have any right, title or interest" cannot be determined from the section.

The disclaimer of "any equity or other interest in the assets of the Fund, except as set forth in the Plan" sits against Section 12.15, under which no person has any right to a benefit "unless and until the Board determines" the requirements are met. Whether a Plan-conferred interest exists before a Board determination is unresolved between them.

The amendment substitutes for a fixed 18 percent "such other interest rate that the Trustees deem appropriate given [the] circumstance[s]," a standard with no cap, floor or benchmark, set by the party collecting. Sections 9.4(a) and 9.7(b), which compute interest "in accordance with" Section 9.5, are left without an ascertainable rate.

The closing sentence reads "The appointment of Trustees shall be selected by the provisions of Section 3.4," a mechanical error for "governed by" that leaves the appointment rule stated ungrammatically and in doubt. Section 3.4 in any event addresses only written appointments and acceptances of successors.

Providing that the Union Trustees "shall be" the incumbent president and vice president/secretary-treasurer cannot be squared with amended Section 3.1's grant to the Union of the power to select its two Trustees, or with Section 3.10, under which the principal officer designates a successor. Whether an office-holder automatically becomes a Trustee is left unresolved among these provisions.
